cards.title: Income minus costs is your surplus
cards.body: A budget starts with two lists: what comes in each month (net pay, after tax) and what goes out. Subtract the costs from the income. What is left is your surplus: the money you can save or invest. If it is negative, you are spending more than you earn, and the gap is paid by savings or debt.
cards.example: Net pay 5,800 PLN; rent 2,000, food 1,200, bills 500, transport 300, phone and internet 100. Costs 4,100 PLN, surplus 1,700 PLN.

links.title: Budgeting: How to create a budget and stick with it (blog, 5 June 2019, archived)

cards.title: Fixed and variable costs
cards.body: Fixed costs are the same every month: rent, a loan instalment, a subscription. Variable costs change: groceries, fuel, eating out. Fixed costs are hard to cut quickly, so they set the floor of your budget. Variable costs are where you can adjust when money is tight.
cards.example: If fixed costs are 3,000 PLN and variable costs 1,500 PLN, cutting variable costs by a fifth saves 300 PLN a month; fixed costs stay at 3,000.

links.title: Module 1: How do I prepare a budget?

cards.title: Spread yearly costs over the months
cards.body: Some costs come once or twice a year: insurance, car service, school things, holidays. If you plan only for monthly bills, these feel like surprises. Divide each yearly cost by 12 and set that amount aside every month, so the money is there when the bill arrives.
cards.example: A 2,400 PLN yearly bill is 200 PLN a month. Three such bills add 600 PLN to your monthly costs.

links.title: Module 1: How do I prepare a budget?

question.q: Net pay is 6,500 PLN a month. Rent 2,200, food 1,400, bills 600, transport 400 and a loan instalment 500. What is left each month?
Car insurance costs 1,800 PLN once a year. How much should you put aside each month so it is not a surprise?

reveal.why: 1,800 / 12 = 150 PLN a month. Spreading yearly costs over the months keeps the budget honest.

question.q: Which of these is a fixed monthly cost?
options: Rent
Eating out
A weekend trip

reveal.why: Rent is the same every month. Eating out and trips change, so they are variable costs.

cards.title: Inflation: the same money buys less
cards.body: Inflation is the rise in prices of what households buy. In Poland, the statistics office (GUS) measures it every month from a fixed basket of goods and services. When prices rise, each zloty buys a little less, even if the number on your account stays the same.
cards.example: In December 2019, prices in Poland were 3.4% higher than a year earlier (GUS). 100 PLN then bought what about 96.70 PLN had bought a year before.

links.title: Miesięczne wskaźniki cen towarów i usług konsumpcyjnych od 1982 roku (CPI, monthly)
What is inflation?

cards.title: Real return: interest minus inflation
cards.body: What matters is not how much your balance grows, but how much more it can buy. A quick rule: real return is about the interest rate minus inflation. If inflation is higher than the rate you earn, your savings lose buying power even while the balance grows.
cards.example: An account pays 3% a year and prices rise 5%. 10,000 PLN becomes 10,300 PLN, but buys about 1.9% less than a year earlier.

cards.title: Reading the inflation number
cards.body: The headline inflation rate compares prices with the same month a year earlier. A rate of 3% means prices are 3% higher than twelve months ago, not that they rose 3% this month. When the rate falls, prices are still rising, only more slowly. Prices fall only when the rate is below zero.
cards.example: Poland, 2020 (GUS): the rate fell from 4.6% in March to 2.4% in December, yet prices in December were still 2.4% higher than a year earlier.

links.title: Miesięczne wskaźniki cen towarów i usług konsumpcyjnych od 1982 roku (CPI, monthly)
What is inflation?

question.q: Prices rise 10% in a year. A shopping basket cost 200 PLN. What does the same basket cost a year later?
A savings account pays 2% a year and prices rise 5%. After a year, what can your money buy?
options: More than today
Exactly the same as today
Less than today

reveal.why: Your balance grows 2%, but prices grow 5%, so the same money buys about 3% less.

question.q: If the balance on your account grows, your buying power always grows too.

reveal.why: Not if prices rise faster than your balance. What counts is what the money buys.

cards.title: Interest on interest
cards.body: With compound interest, the interest you earn is added to the balance, and next year it earns interest too. The growth starts slowly and then speeds up, because each year adds a percentage of a bigger amount. With simple interest, you earn the same amount every year.
cards.example: 2,000 PLN at 6% a year for 10 years: about 3,582 PLN with interest added each year, 3,200 PLN if the interest is paid out.

links.title: Tips for Teaching Students About Saving and Investing
How Does Compound Interest Work? (Open Vault blog, 12 September 2018)
links.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

cards.title: Time matters most
cards.body: Because growth speeds up over time, the years your money stays invested count more than the amount you add later. Starting early gives compounding more years to work. Waiting ten years can cost more than a much lower monthly amount would.
cards.example: 200 PLN a month at 5% a year (added monthly) until 65: starting at 25 gives about 305,000 PLN from 96,000 paid in; starting at 35 gives about 166,000 PLN from 72,000.

links.title: Tips for Teaching Students About Saving and Investing
How Does Compound Interest Work? (Open Vault blog, 12 September 2018)
links.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

cards.title: The rule of 72
cards.body: A quick way to see compounding: divide 72 by the yearly rate to get roughly how many years it takes for money to double. It works the other way too: at a given inflation rate, it tells you how fast prices double, so your cash buys half as much.
cards.example: At 6% a year, money doubles in about 72 / 6 = 12 years (exactly 11.9). At 3% inflation, prices double in about 24 years.

links.title: Tips for Teaching Students About Saving and Investing

question.q: You put 1,000 PLN in an account that pays 10% a year, and the interest is added each year. How much is there after 2 years?

reveal.why: Year 1: 1,000 + 100 = 1,100. Year 2: 1,100 + 110 = 1,210. The second year's interest is earned on the first year's interest too.

question.q: Two accounts both pay 5% a year on 1,000 PLN for 10 years. One adds the interest to the balance each year, the other pays it out. Which ends with more in total?
options: The one that adds interest to the balance
Both end the same
The one that pays it out

reveal.why: When interest stays in the account, it earns interest itself: about 1,629 PLN vs 1,500 PLN after 10 years.

strings: The one that adds interest to the balance

question.q: With compound interest, starting five years earlier can matter more than a slightly higher rate.

reveal.why: Time multiplies the effect: every extra year adds interest on all the interest earned so far.

checked.f3.c2: Future value of 200 PLN a month, r = 5%/12: n = 480 -> 305,204; n = 360 -> 166,452 (Claude, 2026-11-21). Illustrative rate, not a forecast.

nodes.title: Risk as a spread of outcomes

cards.title: Risk is a spread of outcomes
cards.body: Risk is not only "losing money". It is how wide the range of possible results is. A deposit gives almost the same result every year. Shares give a much wider range: some years far above average, some far below. Before you invest, look at the bad years, not only the average.
cards.example: US shares with dividends, 1976-2025: best year +37.2%, worst year -36.6% (2008). In a year like 2008, 10,000 PLN would have become about 6,345 PLN (ignoring the currency).

links.title: Historical returns on stocks, bonds and bills: 1928-2025

cards.title: Higher expected return, wider spread
cards.body: Investments expected to earn more usually come with a wider spread of results; that is the price of the higher average. In an EU survey in 2023, 57% of adults in Poland answered the risk-and-return question correctly. Knowing this protects you from offers that promise high returns with no risk.
cards.example: 1976-2025, worst year: US shares -36.6%, 10-year US Treasury bonds -17.8%, a 50/50 mix of the two -17.9%.

links.title: Historical returns on stocks, bonds and bills: 1928-2025
Flash Eurobarometer 525: Monitoring the level of financial literacy in the EU, volume C (Poland, weighted)

cards.title: A bad outcome is not always a bad decision
cards.body: Because results are spread, a sensible choice can still have a bad year, and a reckless one can get lucky. Judge a decision by what you knew and by the range of outcomes it faced, not only by how it turned out. This app grades your reasons and shows the outcome separately.
cards.example: Shares bought at the start of 2008 lost 36.6% that year (US shares), and were back above the starting value by the end of 2012.

links.title: Historical returns on stocks, bonds and bills: 1928-2025

question.q: In investing, what does risk mean?
options: Only the chance of losing everything
How wide the range of possible results is
How much the investment costs

reveal.why: Risk is the spread of outcomes: a deposit gives almost the same result each year, shares a much wider range.

strings: How wide the range of possible results is

question.q: A sensible decision can still have a bad outcome.

reveal.why: Because results are spread, a good choice can have a bad year. Judge a decision by what you knew and the range of outcomes.

question.q: Which of these are warning signs in an investment offer? Pick all that apply.
options: It promises high returns with no risk
It shows the worst years as well as the average
It shows only the average result
It says returns are guaranteed and much higher than a deposit

reveal.why: Higher expected returns come with a wider spread. An offer that hides the bad years, or promises high returns with no risk, is a warning sign.

strings: It promises high returns with no risk
It shows only the average result
It says returns are guaranteed and much higher than a deposit

cards.title: Bank deposits
cards.body: A bank deposit pays a rate that is fixed for its term, for example 3, 6 or 12 months. If you break it early, you usually lose some or all of the interest. Money in Polish banks and credit unions is guaranteed by the Bank Guarantee Fund (BFG) up to the PLN equivalent of EUR 100,000 per person in each bank.
cards.example: 10,000 PLN on a 12-month deposit at an illustrative 5% earns 500 PLN before tax.

links.title: Wysokość gwarancji
Gwarantowanie depozytów

cards.title: Polish retail Treasury bonds
cards.body: The State Treasury sells savings bonds at 100 PLN each, with no buying fee. Some pay a rate fixed for the whole term (TOS, 3 years). Some have a floating rate (ROR, DOR). Others follow inflation after the first year (COI 4 years, EDO 10 years, and the family bonds ROS and ROD). You can sell them back early for a small fee per bond, taken from the interest.
cards.example: Early redemption fee per 100 PLN bond (bought from September 2024): ROR 0.50, DOR 0.70, TOS 1.00, COI 2.00, EDO 3.00 PLN. Current rates: see obligacjeskarbowe.pl.

links.title: Obligacje skarbowe: current offer
Obligacje skarbowe: FAQ

cards.title: Bonds vs funds: who pays the tax
cards.body: Interest on Polish retail Treasury bonds is taxed at 19%, and the tax is taken automatically, so you do not report it in your annual return. Gains on fund units are also taxed at 19%, but since 2024 you settle them yourself in PIT-38. The bonds are backed by the State Treasury and are kept in a register, so they cannot be lost or stolen.
cards.example: 100 PLN of interest on bonds: 19 PLN tax withheld, 81 PLN paid out.

links.title: Obligacje skarbowe: FAQ
Zbycie jednostek uczestnictwa w funduszu kapitałowym

cards.title: Real return: what your money buys
cards.body: What counts is what your money can buy. If it earns 5% while prices rise 3%, it buys only about 2% more. If prices rise faster than your rate, you lose buying power even though the balance grows. Inflation-indexed bonds are built to follow prices; fixed-rate ones are not. In a 2023 EU survey, 68% of adults in Poland answered the inflation question correctly.
cards.example: 5% interest, 3% inflation: 10,000 PLN becomes 10,500 PLN, which buys what about 10,194 PLN bought a year earlier.

links.title: 10-year inflation-indexed retail bond EDO (series EDO1136)
Flash Eurobarometer 525: Monitoring the level of financial literacy in the EU, volume C (Poland, weighted)

question.q: Up to what amount does the Bank Guarantee Fund (BFG) protect money in one Polish bank, per person?
options: The PLN equivalent of EUR 100,000
There is no limit

reveal.why: The BFG guarantees up to the PLN equivalent of EUR 100,000 per person in each bank.

question.q: Your deposit earns 5% in a year while prices rise 3%. By about how many percent does your buying power grow?

reveal.why: 10,500 PLN buys what about 10,194 PLN bought a year earlier (10,500 / 1.03), so about 2% more, not 5%.

question.q: Which Polish retail Treasury bond follows inflation after its first year?
options: TOS (3 years, fixed rate)
EDO (10 years)
ROR (floating rate)

reveal.why: COI, EDO and the family bonds ROS and ROD follow inflation after the first year. TOS is fixed; ROR floats with the rate.

cards.title: One company or a basket
cards.body: An index is a basket of many companies, for example the largest companies on one stock exchange. One company can fail, and its shares can fall to zero. For a whole index to do that, all its companies would have to fail at once. An index fund lets you own the whole basket in one purchase. In a 2023 EU survey, 54% of adults in Poland answered the diversification question correctly.
cards.example: 10,000 PLN in one company can become 0 PLN. In a broad index, 2008 turned 10,000 into about 6,345 (US shares), and the index was back above its start by the end of 2012.

links.title: Flash Eurobarometer 525: Monitoring the level of financial literacy in the EU, volume C (Poland, weighted)
Historical returns on stocks, bonds and bills: 1928-2025

cards.title: What spreading cannot remove
cards.body: Owning many companies removes the risk of one company failing. It does not remove the risk of the whole market falling. In 2008 the US market (S&P 500 with dividends) fell 36.6%, and owning 500 companies did not prevent that. That is why portfolios also mix in other kinds of investments (node P1).
cards.example: One company: 10,000 PLN can become 0. Whole market in 2008: about 6,345.

links.title: Historical returns on stocks, bonds and bills: 1928-2025

question.q: Why can one company's shares fall to zero while a broad index rarely does?
options: Indexes are protected by the state
For an index to reach zero, all its companies would have to fail at once
The stock exchange fixes index prices

reveal.why: An index is a basket of many companies. One can fail; all failing at once is very unlikely.

strings: For an index to reach zero, all its companies would have to fail at once

question.q: Owning many companies protects you from the whole market falling.

reveal.why: Spreading removes the risk of one company failing, not of the whole market falling: in 2008 the S&P 500 fell 36.6%.

question.q: A friend has all their savings in one company they like. What would you ask them first?
options: What happens to your savings if that company fails?
How much has it gone up this year?
Which company is it?

feedback: A good first question: it points at the risk that spreading would remove.
Past gains say little about the risk of keeping everything in one place.
Natural to ask, but the bigger question is how much depends on one company.

checked.i4.c1: EB525 vol. C Poland Q6: 53.5% correct. 2008 and recovery: Damodaran table (cumulative 1.086 at end of 2012). Definition of an index: reviewer to add a source.

cards.title: What a fund is
cards.body: A fund pools money from many people and invests it according to a stated policy. You own units, and their value follows what the fund holds. An ETF is a fund whose units are traded on a stock exchange, like shares. In the EU, many investment products come with a Key Information Document (KID) of at most three A4 pages.
cards.example: Buy 1,000 PLN of units; if the fund's holdings rise 5%, your units are worth about 1,050 PLN before costs.

links.title: Regulation (EU) No 1286/2014 on key information documents for PRIIPs

cards.title: Costs grow over time
cards.body: Fund costs are taken from your money every year, so they compound like returns do, only against you. A difference that looks small per year becomes large over decades. Compare the "What are the costs?" section of two KIDs before you compare their past results.
cards.example: 50,000 PLN for 20 years at 6% a year before costs: with 2% yearly costs it grows to about 109,556 PLN; with 0.3% to about 151,520 PLN. The difference is 41,964 PLN.

links.title: Regulation (EU) No 1286/2014 on key information documents for PRIIPs

cards.title: How to read a KID
cards.body: Every KID has the same sections in the same order. What is this product? What are the risks and what could I get in return? What happens if the manufacturer is unable to pay out? What are the costs? How long should I hold it and can I take money out early? How can I complain? The fixed order lets you compare two products side by side.
cards.example: Put two KIDs next to each other and read only 'What are the costs?' first.

links.title: Regulation (EU) No 1286/2014 on key information documents for PRIIPs

cards.title: Tax on fund gains in Poland
cards.body: A gain from selling or redeeming fund units is taxed at 19%. Since 2024 you settle it yourself in the PIT-38 tax return. A loss can reduce gains from the same source in the following years. IKE and IKZE accounts have their own rules (node L1).
cards.example: Units bought for 10,000 PLN and sold for 12,000 PLN: gain 2,000 PLN, tax 380 PLN.

links.title: Zbycie jednostek uczestnictwa w funduszu kapitałowym

question.q: What is an ETF?
options: A fund whose units are traded on a stock exchange, like shares
A type of bank deposit
A government savings bond

reveal.why: An ETF is a fund; its units trade on an exchange, so you can buy a whole basket in one purchase.

strings: A fund whose units are traded on a stock exchange, like shares

question.q: Two funds hold similar investments. Which section of their KIDs should you compare first?
options: What are the costs?
How can I complain?
What happens if the manufacturer is unable to pay out?

reveal.why: Costs are taken every year and compound against you, so compare them before past results.

question.q: You bought fund units for 10,000 PLN and sold them for 12,000 PLN. How much tax is due in Poland?

reveal.why: The gain is 2,000 PLN, taxed at 19%: 380 PLN, settled yourself in PIT-38.

cards.title: Mix things that move differently
cards.body: If two investments do not fall at the same time, holding both gives a smoother ride than holding either alone. In 2008, US shares fell 36.6% while 10-year US Treasury bonds gained 20.1%. A 50/50 mix of the two lost about 8%.
cards.example: 10,000 PLN split 50/50 in 2008 ended at about 9,178, instead of about 6,345 in shares only.

links.title: Historical returns on stocks, bonds and bills: 1928-2025

cards.title: Correlation in plain words
cards.body: Correlation says whether two investments tend to move together. If they move together, mixing them protects you little. If they move apart, or without a link, mixing smooths the ride. Correlation is not fixed: the ECB notes that the stock-bond correlation was positive from the late 1960s to the late 1990s, negative in the 2000s, and has risen again.
cards.example: Shares and bonds in 2008 moved apart (-36.6% and +20.1%); in 2022 they moved together (-18.0% and -17.8%).

links.title: Cross-asset correlations in a more inflationary environment and challenges for diversification strategies (Financial Stability Review, November 2022)
Historical returns on stocks, bonds and bills: 1928-2025

cards.title: 2022: when both fell
cards.body: In 2022, US shares fell 18.0% and 10-year US Treasury bonds fell 17.8%. The ECB linked the rise in stock-bond correlation to inflation and to central banks raising rates. It warned that a higher correlation can make a mixed portfolio look less risky than it is.
cards.example: A 50/50 mix lost about 17.9% in 2022, close to shares alone.

links.title: Cross-asset correlations in a more inflationary environment and challenges for diversification strategies (Financial Stability Review, November 2022)
Historical returns on stocks, bonds and bills: 1928-2025

question.q: Why mix shares and bonds in one portfolio?
options: They always rise together
They often don't fall at the same time, which smooths the ride
Mixing removes all risk

reveal.why: In 2008 shares fell 36.6% while 10-year US bonds gained 20.1%; a 50/50 mix lost only about 8%.

strings: They often don't fall at the same time, which smooths the ride

question.q: The link (correlation) between shares and bonds stays the same over time.

reveal.why: They moved apart in 2008 and together in 2022. The ECB notes the correlation has changed sign over the decades.

question.q: In 2022 a 50/50 mix of US shares and bonds lost almost as much as shares alone. Why?
options: Shares and bonds fell together as inflation and interest rates rose
The bonds in the mix defaulted
The mix was rebalanced too often

reveal.why: Both fell about 18%. The ECB links the higher correlation to inflation and rising central-bank rates.

strings: Shares and bonds fell together as inflation and interest rates rose

checked.p1.c3: ECB FSR box: 'might be related to inflationary pressures', 'initial underestimation of portfolio risk'. 2022: stocks -18.04%, T-bond -17.83%, 50/50 -17.94% (Damodaran table).

cards.title: Time changes how much risk you can carry
cards.body: Shares can lose a lot in one bad year, but over longer periods the bad years have been offset more often. In US history since 1928, shares with dividends lost money in about a quarter of single years, in about one in eight 5-year periods, and in none of the 20-year periods. Money you need soon cannot wait for a recovery.
cards.example: US shares, 1928-2025: losses in 26 of 98 single years, 11 of 94 five-year periods, 5 of 89 ten-year periods, 0 of 79 twenty-year periods. The worst 3-year period lost 62%.

links.title: Historical returns on stocks, bonds and bills: 1928-2025

cards.title: One goal, one horizon, one mix
cards.body: Give each goal its own mix. Money for a goal two years away belongs mostly in deposits or bonds, because a bad year in shares could leave you short. A goal 30 years away can hold more shares, because there is time to recover. As the goal comes closer, move part of the money into safer assets step by step.
cards.example: In US history, a 50/50 mix of shares and 10-year bonds lost money in 4 of 94 five-year periods; the worst lost 17%. Shares alone: 11 of 94, worst 49%.

links.title: Historical returns on stocks, bonds and bills: 1928-2025

cards.title: History is a guide, not a promise
cards.body: These figures come from one country, the US, in one century, and they ignore inflation. Other markets have had longer bad stretches, and the Polish stock market has a much shorter history. "No 20-year loss so far" does not mean it cannot happen. Use history to understand the spread of outcomes, not to predict your result.
cards.example: 0 of 79 twenty-year periods lost money in US shares; that is a record, not a guarantee.

links.title: Historical returns on stocks, bonds and bills: 1928-2025

question.q: You need the money for a flat deposit in two years. Where does most of it belong?
options: Mostly in shares, because they earn the most
Mostly in deposits or bonds
All in one fast-growing company

reveal.why: A goal two years away can't wait for a recovery after a bad year in shares, so it belongs mostly in safer assets.

question.q: In US history, shares with dividends have never lost money over a 20-year period, so it can never happen.

reveal.why: 0 of 79 twenty-year periods lost money in US shares, but that is one country's record, not a guarantee.

question.q: As a long-term goal comes closer, what does a horizon-based plan usually do?
options: Moves part of the money into safer assets step by step
Moves everything into shares to catch up
Leaves the mix unchanged until the last day

reveal.why: The shorter the time left, the less room there is to recover from a fall, so the mix shifts gradually towards safer assets.

strings: Moves part of the money into safer assets step by step

nodes.title: Rebalancing and discipline in a crash

cards.title: Rebalancing
cards.body: You choose a target mix, for example 60% shares and 40% bonds. Markets move your mix away from it. Rebalancing means returning to the target from time to time: selling some of what grew and buying what fell. It is a rule decided in calm times, so you do not have to decide in a panic.
cards.example: Target 60/40 on 10,000 PLN. Shares fall and the mix becomes 50/50 at 8,000 PLN; rebalancing moves 800 PLN from bonds to shares to get back to 60/40.

cards.title: Selling after a fall locks in the loss
cards.body: A fall is a loss on paper until you sell. In 2008, US shares (S&P 500 with dividends) fell 36.6%; in 2009 they rose 25.9%. Someone who sold at the end of 2008 kept the loss and missed the rebound. Someone who kept a rule, holding or rebalancing, did not.
cards.example: 10,000 PLN in US shares at the start of 2008: about 6,345 at the end of 2008, about 7,991 at the end of 2009 if held (ignoring the currency).

links.title: Historical returns on stocks, bonds and bills: 1928-2025

cards.title: Write your rule before the storm
cards.body: Decide now what you will do if your investments fall 20% or 30%: hold, rebalance, or, if your goal is near, move to safer assets on a schedule. A rule written in advance protects you from fear and from headlines. The hard task in this node lets you test your rule on past crashes.
cards.example: My rule: if shares are more than 10 points away from 60%, rebalance once, at the end of the month.

question.q: What does rebalancing a 60/40 portfolio mean?
options: Selling everything after a fall
Returning to the 60/40 target by selling some of what grew and buying what fell
Moving everything to what did best last year

reveal.why: Rebalancing returns the mix to its target from time to time, following a rule set in calm times.

strings: Returning to the 60/40 target by selling some of what grew and buying what fell

question.q: Your target is 60% shares. After a fall your portfolio is worth 8,000 PLN, with 4,000 PLN in shares. How much must move into shares to get back to 60%?

reveal.why: 60% of 8,000 is 4,800 PLN. Shares are at 4,000, so 800 PLN moves from bonds to shares.

question.q: Your investments fell 25% in a month. What do you do?
options: Follow the rule I wrote down in advance
Sell everything before it falls further
Buy more of whatever fell most, without a plan

feedback: That is the point of a rule: it protects you from deciding in a panic.
Selling after a fall locks in the loss. After 2008, those who sold at the bottom missed the rebound in 2009.
Acting without a plan is the same problem in the other direction. A written rule is calmer.

cards.title: What an emergency fund is
cards.body: An emergency fund is money you keep only for surprises: a car repair, a medical bill, or a month without pay. Without it, a surprise often ends on a credit card or a quick loan, which costs much more than the surprise itself. Keep it apart from spending money and from investments, so it is there when you need it.
cards.example: Ania spends 4,800 PLN a month. A 3,000 PLN car repair equals about 19 days of her costs.

links.title: An essential guide to building an emergency fund

cards.title: How big should it be?
cards.body: There is no single right number; it depends on your situation. Start from your essential monthly costs: rent, food, bills, loan instalments. Then ask how many months you would need to find new income. A steady job and no dependants need fewer months. Irregular income, or one earner in a family, needs more. Even a small buffer helps, so build one month first.
cards.example: Essential costs 4,800 PLN x 3 months = 14,400 PLN. Saving 600 PLN a month, that takes 24 months.

links.title: An essential guide to building an emergency fund

cards.title: Where to keep it
cards.body: Somewhere safe and quick to reach, such as a savings account or a short bank deposit. Not in shares or crypto, because their value can fall exactly when you need the money. In Poland, money in domestic banks and credit unions is guaranteed by the Bank Guarantee Fund (BFG) up to the PLN equivalent of EUR 100,000 per person in each bank.
cards.example: A 14,400 PLN buffer in one Polish bank is fully within the guarantee.

links.title: Wysokość gwarancji
Gwarantowanie depozytów

cards.title: You are not alone
cards.body: In an EU survey in 2023, 30% of adults in Poland said they had no emergency savings, or could cover their costs for less than a month without income. Among 18-24-year-olds it was 42%. Building a buffer is the first step, before investing.
cards.example: Of 10 young adults in Poland, about 4 could not last a month without income.
